claims.sentence: An ultrasound scan uses high-frequency sound waves to make a picture of the inside of the body.
claims.evidence: Search text: probe emits high-frequency sound waves, echoes from body structures converted into a moving image.

claims.sentence: The sound waves bounce off different parts of the body, and the echoes are picked up by a probe and turned into a moving image.
claims.evidence: Same: sound waves reflect off structures; computer builds picture; moving image.

claims.sentence: It does not use radiation or X-rays.
claims.evidence: NHS: ultrasound scans do not use radiation, unlike X-rays or CT.

claims.sentence: NHS pages say it helps doctors to examine symptoms, to see inside the body during other procedures, and to monitor pregnancy.
claims.evidence: Retrieved NHS text covered pregnancy scans and guidance of biopsy/drainage, not the three-part statement attributed to NHS pages.
claims.newSentence: NHS and NHS trust pages describe ultrasound being used to look inside the body, to guide procedures such as biopsy and drainage, and during pregnancy.

claims.sentence: It can also help to guide a biopsy or the draining of fluid.
claims.evidence: Royal Marsden: biopsy performed under ultrasound guidance; image-guided drainage of fluid or abscess uses ultrasound or CT guidance.

claims.sentence: Ultrasound is generally less effective than CT or MRI at imaging through bone or air.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text compares ultrasound with CT or MRI through bone or air.

claims.sentence: The person lies on a couch, and the room may be dimmed so the screen is easier to see.
claims.evidence: Couch and dimmed room not found in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: Gel is put on the skin over the area, and the sonographer or radiologist moves a small probe over it while watching the pictures.
claims.evidence: Gel on skin and probe moved across skin supported; sonographer/radiologist watching pictures not stated verbatim.
claims.newSentence: Gel is put on the skin over the area and a small probe is moved across it.

claims.sentence: The gel is water-based and washes off easily, and trust leaflets say it will not stain clothing.
claims.evidence: Trust text: water-based gel, wipe off with paper towel, one trust says it dissolves in water and will not stain clothing.

claims.sentence: Trust leaflets say the scan takes about 20 minutes in many cases, though the length depends on the area examined.
claims.evidence: NHS page says around 10 to 45 minutes, possibly longer; trusts give 10 to 30 minutes. About 20 minutes not found.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says an ultrasound scan takes around 10 to 45 minutes, and may take longer.

claims.sentence: Afterwards the gel is wiped off, the person can get dressed, and they can usually leave straight away.
claims.evidence: Wipe gel off and get dressed supported; leaving straight away not stated.
claims.newSentence: Afterwards the gel can be wiped off and the person can get dressed.

claims.sentence: For scans of the pelvis, kidneys or bladder, people are usually asked to arrive with a full bladder.
claims.evidence: Full bladder supported for pelvic and bladder scans (trust pages: drink water, do not empty bladder). Kidneys were listed under fasting, not full bladder.
claims.newSentence: For pelvic and bladder scans, people are usually asked to arrive with a full bladder.

claims.sentence: One trust explains that a full bladder pushes the womb into a position that is easier to scan.
claims.evidence: Retrieved reason: sound waves travel more easily through fluid (urine), giving a clearer picture. Womb positioning not found.
claims.newSentence: Trust leaflets explain that a full bladder gives a clearer picture because sound waves travel more easily through fluid.

claims.sentence: Leaflets ask people not to pass urine until after the scan, and say that anyone who becomes uncomfortably full during the scan can tell the staff and may be able to leave the room to empty their bladder before it is finished.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: do not empty bladder until after the scan; full bladder may be a little uncomfortable; toilet nearby afterwards. Leaving mid-scan not found.
claims.newSentence: Leaflets ask people not to empty their bladder until after the scan, and say a toilet is nearby afterwards.

claims.sentence: Scans of some organs, such as the liver, may need no food for several hours beforehand.
claims.evidence: Search: for abdominal scans (liver, gallbladder, kidneys) people are usually asked not to eat for several hours.

claims.sentence: The appointment letter gives the exact instructions for each type of scan.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: the hospital or clinic should tell you how to prepare. Appointment letter specifically not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The hospital or clinic tells people how to prepare for their type of scan.

claims.sentence: The usual scan is external, with the probe on the skin.
claims.evidence: Trust pages: external scan with probe moved across the skin; transvaginal is the internal alternative.

claims.sentence: Some people have a transvaginal (internal) scan to provide more information about the pelvis.
claims.evidence: Transvaginal scans exist and are used more in early pregnancy; "more information about the pelvis" not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Some people have a transvaginal (internal) scan.

claims.sentence: For this scan the probe is disinfected, covered with a protective sheath and lubricated with gel.
claims.evidence: Trusts: probe cleaned, covered with protective sheath, lubricated with jelly/gel.

claims.sentence: People usually need to empty their bladder first for an internal scan.
claims.evidence: Several trusts say to empty the bladder first for a transvaginal scan.

claims.sentence: A bladder scan is a quick scan that measures the volume of urine in the bladder, and it is often used to check how well the bladder empties.
claims.evidence: No NHS bladder-scan page retrieved; only a research article.

claims.sentence: Ultrasound can also be used to look at blood flow and at whether blood vessels are narrowed or blocked.
claims.evidence: Royal Marsden: ultrasound can detect blood flow and any narrowing or blockage of blood vessels.

claims.sentence: NHS leaflets describe ultrasound as safe and low risk, and one says it does not use radiation.
claims.evidence: NHS says the sound waves are safe and ultrasound uses no radiation; "low risk" wording not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says the sound waves used in ultrasound scans are safe, and that ultrasound scans do not use radiation.

claims.sentence: The NHS pregnancy pages describe scans as painless and with no known side effects.
claims.evidence: An NHS maternity leaflet says scans are painless with no known side effects; NHS says no known risks from the sound waves. Not stated on the cited nhs.uk pregnancy page in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: An NHS maternity leaflet says scans are painless and have no known side effects.

claims.sentence: A possible minor problem is skin irritation or infection from the gel, which wiping the gel off thoroughly after the scan helps to prevent, according to one leaflet.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: standard gel is not sterile so there is a very small risk of infection in some circumstances. Skin irritation and prevention by wiping not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: One hospital notes that standard ultrasound gel is not sterile, so there is a very small risk of infection in some circumstances.

claims.sentence: People with a latex allergy are asked to tell the department beforehand so latex-free products can be used.
claims.evidence: NHS: people with a latex allergy should tell staff so an alternative can be used.

claims.sentence: A sonographer or radiologist interprets the pictures.
claims.evidence: Royal Marsden leaflet: images reviewed by the specialist who performed the exam; sonographer/radiologist wording not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: The images are reviewed by the specialist who carried out the scan.

claims.sentence: The report goes to the doctor or team who requested the scan.
claims.evidence: Search: result is sent to the doctor who referred you for the scan.

claims.sentence: One trust says the findings are combined with other clinical information and discussed with the person as part of their treatment plan.
claims.evidence: Not found in retrieved text.

claims.sentence: How soon a report is ready depends on the local service, and one trust says most reports are ready 24 hours after the scan.
claims.evidence: NHS: results may be given at the end of the appointment or take a few weeks depending on the reason for the scan; one trust says within 1 week for GP referrals. 24 hours not found.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says results may be given at the end of the appointment, or can take a few weeks, depending on the reason for the scan.

claims.sentence: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves rather than radiation, and NHS leaflets describe it as low risk.
claims.evidence: Sound waves not radiation supported; "low risk" not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves rather than radiation, and the NHS describes the sound waves used as safe.

claims.sentence: A water-based gel goes on the skin, and a small probe is moved over the area being scanned.
claims.evidence: Water-based gel and probe moved over skin supported.

claims.sentence: Scans of the pelvis, kidneys or bladder usually need a full bladder, and the appointment letter explains this.
claims.evidence: Full bladder supported for pelvic and bladder scans only; appointment letter not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: Pelvic and bladder scans usually need a full bladder, and the hospital or clinic explains how to prepare.

claims.sentence: Some people have an internal (transvaginal) scan to give more information.
claims.evidence: Transvaginal scan exists; purpose "to give more information" not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Some people have an internal (transvaginal) scan.

claims.sentence: An ultrasound scan uses sound waves, not radiation, to make live pictures. This guide covers the gel, the full bladder, internal scans and results.
claims.evidence: Descriptive of guide; sound waves, no radiation, moving image supported. Edited topics (results) remain in the guide.

notes: Retrieval was thin (search summaries, few verbatim page texts); strict classification applied. Extra facts: Duration 10-45 min, results same day or few weeks: https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/ultrasound-scan/ | Transvaginal probe covered with sheath, bladder emptied first: https://www.uhsussex.nhs.uk/resources/transvaginal-ultrasound-examination/ | Gel not sterile, very small infection risk: https://dchft.nhs.uk/leaflets/ultrasound-scan/ (approximate; hospital page from search 1) | Latex allergy: tell staff: https://www.nhs.uk/tests-and-treatments/ultrasound-scan/
